proposals.label: Corbett et al. (2019)
proposals.rationale: The entry has only linkage to 2p11.1-q12.2 and no variants. Corbett et al. (2019) identified the causal mutation, an intronic ATTTC pentamer repeat insertion/expansion in STARD7, in 158 individuals from 22 families. The paper also reports anticipation, finds the expansion in families carrying the ADRA2B variant (arguing that variant is not causal), finds no effect on STARD7 expression, and describes a diagnostic RP-PCR assay.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized clinical data from 22 FAME families of Australian/New Zealand, Italian, Iraqi and Israeli Sephardic Jewish, South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian origin. Nearly all affected individuals had cortical myoclonic tremor or myoclonus. Onset was usually in the second to third decade. The frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures varied between families from 15 to 100%, and some individuals had focal seizures.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) performed whole-genome sequencing with repeat expansion detection (ExpansionHunter, exSTRa) in affected individuals from an Australian-New Zealand, an Italian, and a French-Spanish FAME family. In intron 1 of the STARD7 gene, within the FAME2 linkage interval on chromosome 2, they identified an expansion of the endogenous ATTTT pentamer repeat with an inserted ATTTC repeat. The ATTTC repeat was absent from WGS data of 69 controls. Using repeat-primed PCR (RP-PCR), they found the expansion in 137 of 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families. They also found it in 20 of 20 familial cases from 6 additional families and in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases with FAME-like phenotypes, for a total of 158 positive individuals from 22 families. Two of 24 unaffected relatives tested carried the expansion and were likely presymptomatic. Eight of 13 individuals with an uncertain diagnosis carried the expansion, and it was absent from 28 control DNAs.

proposals.label: De Fusco et al. (2014)
proposals.rationale: The entry currently has no causal gene or variant. De Fusco et al. (2014) found a heterozygous in-frame indel in ADRA2B that segregated in 2 Tuscan ADCME families sharing a haplotype. They added functional evidence for a gain-of-function mechanism through loss of stable spinophilin binding. They also reported that southern Italian BAFME families linked to the same locus did not carry ADRA2B mutations, which suggests ADCME and BAFME may be distinct entities. The paper also describes a new family with age-related dementia in older carriers and seizures triggered by visual stimuli.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a 4-generation Italian kindred from Tuscany (family B) with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) and 5 affected members, 4 of them living. All patients had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs. Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom and began between ages 18 and 50 years. All but 1 patient had epilepsy, consisting of rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures that were at times precipitated by visual stimuli. Two patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognition and the others had normal intelligence. All patients had generalized or focal paroxysmal EEG activity. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflex studies were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Brain MRI was normal in the patients studied. No patient had cardiovascular disease, and 2 of the oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied a 5-generation Italian family from Tuscany with ADCME, which had previously been mapped to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2. By sequencing candidate genes, they found a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene in affected members (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228). The indel replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) in the third intracellular loop with 4 new residues (QFGR). The mutation segregated completely with the disease. It was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and the 1000 Genomes Project, a total of 16,080 chromosomes. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected family members showed that the ADRA2B mutation was the only relevant change. The same indel was found in a second Tuscan ADCME family (family B). The family history showed no kinship between the 2 families, but they shared the same disease haplotype across the entire critical region, which suggested a common ancestor.

paragraphs.text: Coppola et al. (2016) assessed psychiatric comorbidity in 20 patients from 7 families with autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy (ADCME). They used validated scales (BDI, STAI-Y1/2, MMPI-2, and QoLIE-31) and compared the patients with 20 patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) and 20 healthy controls. Mood disorders were more common in ADCME patients than in either comparison group, particularly depression (p = 0.035 vs JME; p = 0.017 vs controls) and state anxiety. Trait anxiety was higher than in controls but did not differ from that in JME. In ADCME patients, the myoclonus score correlated positively with both state anxiety (rho 0.58) and trait anxiety (rho 0.65). The psychiatric features were often associated with pathological personality traits: paranoid (OR 25.7), psychasthenia (OR 7.0), schizophrenia (OR 8.5), and hypomania (OR 5.5). Lower quality of life correlated with these psychiatric symptoms. The authors recommended a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation at the time of diagnosis.

paragraphs.text: Licchetta et al. (2013) described a large family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor and epilepsy (FCMTE) in which 25 of 127 members were affected (9 males, 16 females). Sixteen living affected members were studied, with a mean age of 47.8 years. Ten (62.5%) of them had cortical myoclonic tremor associated with generalized seizures. Mean age at onset was 28.1 years for tremor and 33.8 years for seizures. Four patients (25%) reported slow progression of the tremor, and 1 of them had severe gait impairment. Psychiatric disorders of variable severity occurred in 37.5%. Polygraphic recordings showed rhythmic bursts at 7 to 15 Hz in all 11 affected members tested. Back-averaging and somatosensory evoked potentials with C-reflex study indicated that the myoclonus was cortical in origin in all patients tested. Generalized epileptiform discharges were recorded in 25% of cases and a photoparoxysmal response in 31%.

proposals.citation: Crompton DE, Sadleir LG, Bromhead CJ, Bahlo M, Bellows ST, Arsov T, Harty R, Lawrence KM, Dunne JW, Berkovic SF, and others. Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy: recognition of mild phenotypes and refinement of the 2q locus. Arch Neurol 69: 474-81, 2012. [PubMed: 22491192]
proposals.label: Crompton et al. (2012)
proposals.rationale: This is the first non-Italian, non-French kindred in the entry, and the largest: 55 affected members of European descent from New Zealand and Australia. It describes a milder spectrum that the entry lacks. The most common picture was a postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, beginning in adolescence (median 15 years, range 4 to 60), with subtle proximal myoclonus. Seizures were uncommon (15%) and came around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus. The paper also narrows the chromosome 2 locus to 13.3 Mb containing 99 protein-coding genes.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, which usually began in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median 17 years; range 5-60). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76). They were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset, after severe generalized myoclonus. Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. Crompton et al. (2012) concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, together with subtle proximal myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: Martí-Massó et al. (2013) studied a Spanish family with autosomal dominant familial cortical myoclonic tremor and epilepsy (FCMTE). Using whole-exome sequencing, they identified a heterozygous nonsense variant in the ACMSD gene (c.77G>A, p.Trp26Ter), located on chromosome 2q21.3. Because ACMSD lies close to the FCMTE2 locus, they sequenced the entire ACMSD coding region and splice sites in 2 families previously linked to FCMTE2 and found no mutations. They concluded that ACMSD is not responsible for the FCMTE2 phenotype and that the FCMTE2 gene remained to be discovered.

evidence.statement: Martí-Massó et al. (2013) described a large Spanish family from northern Spain with autosomal dominant familial cortical myoclonic tremor and epilepsy (FCMTE), with 7 affected individuals over 3 generations; 4 were fully examined. Affected members had seizures (myoclonic and generalized, onset mostly in the teens to early twenties) and postural hand tremor, which in 1 patient was shown on EMG to be myoclonus. One patient (II-3) also developed photosensitive myoclonic seizures, levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with orthostatic tremor, mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 19/30), giant SEPs, bilateral C-reflexes, generalized spike-and-wave EEG discharges, mild cerebellar atrophy, and MRI changes suggesting corticospinal tract wallerian degeneration. Valproate made the tremor worse in 2 patients.

evidence.statement: Martí-Massó et al. (2013) performed whole-exome sequencing in 3 affected members of the Spanish FCMTE family. They found 2 heterozygous variants that segregated with disease: a nonsense variant in ACMSD (c.77G>A, p.Trp26Ter) on chromosome 2q21.3 and a missense variant in MYBBP1A (c.2758G>A, p.Ala920Thr). Both were absent from 188 ethnically matched control chromosomes and from more than 10,000 controls, but only the ACMSD variant was predicted to be pathogenic. ACMSD p.Trp26Ter was not found in 11 familial and 58 sporadic essential tremor cases or in 54 sporadic late-onset Parkinson disease cases.
